source.title: Spectral Superposition: A Theory of Feature Geometry
source.authors: G. Ivanov; N. Oozeer; Shivam Raval; Tasana Pejovic; S. Upadhyay; Amir Abdullah

record.file_problem: The text appears cut off in Appendix I after Figure 39; the main text and earlier appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests superposition-related capacity and feature localization in toy networks using spectral measures and a parameter sweep, rather than measuring neuron responses to input examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own toy-network results on capacity usage and spectral localization, which bear on V3. Mentions of polysemantic neurons and findings from other papers in Related Work are not rows because they are cited results, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes superposition in the Elhage et al. toy model and applies new spectral tools to describe feature geometry: capacity saturation, spectral localization and tight frames. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The TMS hidden layer it analyzes is a linear projection without a neuron basis, so nothing here can show neurons are polysemantic because of superposition. Its results are about feature geometry, a related construct, and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors propose spectral tools (frame operator, per-feature spectral measure) for basis-invariant study of feature geometry. They prove that capacity saturation in toy superposition models forces spectral localization and tight frames, which classifies the known TMS geometries. They caution that saturation is verified only in toy models and that localization in realistic models is not directly measured.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the toy superposition autoencoder and MSE setup attributed to Elhage et al., with a new high-throughput parameter sweep and spectral-localization analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that sparsity changes localization: lower sparsity yields tighter feature configurations, while high sparsity yields more diffuse spectral measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 3,200 toy-model runs (n=1024, m in [16,512], sparsity in [0,0.99]), the sum of feature fractional dimensionalities is approximately m, i.e. capacity is nearly saturated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy superposition models use nearly all hidden-dimension capacity (ΣDi ≈ m).

fits_no_version.finding: Lower sparsity gives tighter, more spectrally localized feature clusters. Higher sparsity gives more diffuse spectral measures, with a small delocalized residue of features that carries little leverage mass.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature spectral localization in superposition decreases with input sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: Proof that if capacity is saturated, every feature lies in a single eigenspace of the frame operator WWᵀ. Feature clusters then form tight frames, and the known TMS geometries (simplices, polygons, antiprisms) are classified via association schemes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity saturation forces spectral localization and tight-frame feature geometry.

record.problems: The empirical evidence is limited to toy models. The reported plots do not provide extractable numerical values in the text, and the study does not measure neuron responses to unrelated semantic inputs or test realistic networks.
record.rows_left_out: No own results bearing on the other claim versions were reported. Related Work's descriptions of findings from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: Whether neurons are polysemantic because features outnumber neurons. Superposition is assumed and no neuron basis or neuron responses are measured.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure is only cited (Lecomte et al.) in Related Work.
No variation of activation function or architecture, and no polysemantic-neuron share measured.

record.verdict_notes: The record treated the paper as testing V3. It does not: it presupposes superposition and studies the geometry of feature directions in a non-privileged hidden space. All neuron-polysemanticity statements are cited Related Work. The text is truncated in Appendix I, and the Appendix G figures have placeholder captions only.

versions.untested_parts: Vision-model neuron responses to multiple input kinds.
Polysemanticity rates in language-model MLP neurons and layer differences.
Neuron-level semantic responses to unrelated inputs; whether capacity pressure is necessary for neuron polysemanticity; non-toy and real-model settings.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on polysemantic-neuron share and performance.
Whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or related features.
How the definition or scoring of neuron polysemanticity changes with activation range or explanation method.

rows.subject: toy models of superposition (TMS)

rows.operation_detail: Proved spectral localization conditional on saturation of the fractional-dimensionality capacity bound.
rows.value: For every feature i, the measure collapses to one Dirac mass, μi = δλk; equivalently, FWi = λkWi.
rows.note: This is a conditional theoretical result about feature vectors and eigenspaces, not an empirical measurement of neuron semantics.
rows.check: This is a conditional theorem (if ΣDi = m, features localize to eigenspaces), not an empirical result. It should not be a result row, or should be flagged as theory only. It does not bear on neuron polysemanticity.

relation.reason: It assumes superposition (more features than dimensions) and analyzes the geometry of feature vectors. It never tests whether superposition makes neurons polysemant.

tranche.reason: The paper takes superposition in the Elhage et al. TMS autoencoder as given and applies its own spectral tools to feature geometry. Its hidden layer is a linear projection h = Wx, so it measures no neuron-level polysemanticity and tests no version, including V3.

source_check.notes: There are no verdicts or version links, which is correct. All results concern feature-vector geometry in the TMS ReLU-output autoencoder (linear hidden layer, no neurons), not neuron polysemanticity. r3 and r4 are figure only, and r2 is a theorem. Lecomte et al. on incidental polysemanticity appears only as cited related work (Appendix H).
